summary: Describes using one RSVP reservation to represent many reservations across a transit region, similar to virtual paths in ATM. It covers creating, classifying, sizing, and releasing the aggregate.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of reserving a seat for each kid on the bus, you reserve one big group seat for the whole class.

questions: how does rsvp scale across a diffserv network
subtitle: How one big RSVP reservation can stand in for thousands of small ones across a transit network.

tldr.problem: RSVP makes every router on a path store state and process messages for every individual reservation, which does not scale in the middle of a large network.
tldr.mechanism: Edge routers (an aggregator and a deaggregator) hide the end-to-end RSVP messages from the routers in between by changing the IP protocol number, and set up a single aggregate reservation, identified by a Diff-Serv code point, that carries the summed traffic of many end-to-end flows.
tldr.outcome: Routers inside the region keep state per aggregate reservation and per traffic class instead of per flow. RFC 3175 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5350.

today: RFC 3175 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5350. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the specification of RSVP aggregation.

sections.title: The Problem of Many Small Reservations
sections.content:
RSVP version 1 has no way to group individual reserved sessions into a common class, and the RFC says such aggregation is required for scalability. Each reservation costs a non-trivial amount of message exchange, computation and memory in every router along the way.

RFC 3175 proposes aggregating several end-to-end (E2E) reservations that cross a region and share the same ingress and egress routers into one larger aggregate reservation. The idea is conceptually similar to Virtual Paths in an ATM network.

The RFC is honest about the cost. Aggregation reduces isolation between flows, so one flow may suffer delay from the bursts of another. It cites evidence that aggregation does not hurt mean delay and actually reduces delay in the tail of the distribution, which offsets some of the lost isolation.
sections.plainLanguage: If every kid on a field trip needs their own ticket check at every door, the line never moves. A single group ticket for the whole class keeps things fast, though kids in the group now share the same space.

sections.title: Aggregator, Interior Router and Deaggregator
sections.content:
An aggregation region is a set of RSVP-capable routers. Interfaces are either exterior or interior to the region. For a given E2E flow, three roles exist:

  • The aggregator is the first router to process the E2E Path message as it enters the region, forwarding it from an exterior to an interior interface.
  • The deaggregator is the last router to process it as it leaves, forwarding it from an interior to an exterior interface.
  • An interior router receives the message on an interior interface and sends it out another one, and does neither job.

One router can play different roles for different flows. The aggregator is easy to identify: an E2E Path arrives on an exterior interface and must go out an interior one. Finding the deaggregator is harder. The RFC mentions manual configuration, or an automatic method in which the deaggregator tells the aggregator about itself when the E2E Path leaves the region. The automatic method is not tied to a routing protocol and adapts to route changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a tunnel. The router at the entrance counts everyone in, the router at the exit counts everyone out, and the routers inside the tunnel just let traffic pass without checking every ticket.

sections.title: Hiding Messages and Classifying with DSCPs
sections.content:
Aggregation depends on hiding E2E RSVP messages from routers inside the region. On entry, the IP protocol number of E2E Path, PathTear and ResvConf messages is changed from RSVP (46) to RSVP-E2E-IGNORE (134). Interior routers ignore such messages and forward them as ordinary IP datagrams. The deaggregator restores the number to RSVP. Resv messages need no change because they travel hop by hop between RSVP neighbors anyway.

Meanwhile, the aggregator sends separate aggregate Path messages, using the normal RSVP protocol number, to the deaggregator. The deaggregator answers with aggregate Resv messages. The token buckets of the E2E reservations are summed into the aggregate messages.

Traffic inside the region is classified by Diff-Serv code point (DSCP) rather than per reservation. The RFC presumes a queue or similar component is set aside on each link for each class of aggregated traffic, so classification and scheduling state does not depend on the number of reservations. A session is therefore identified by the destination address plus the DSCP. There can be several aggregate reservations between the same pair of routers, each with its own DSCP and PHB.

Which E2E reservation goes onto which aggregate is a policy decision outside the specification. The RFC gives the decision to the deaggregator, because it is the first to see the E2E Resv, which carries the requested Int-Serv service type.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge routers put a special sticker on each ticket so the routers in the middle ignore it. The middle routers only look at the color of the wristband (the DSCP) to decide which lane everyone goes in.

sections.title: The Signalling Procedures
sections.content:
The aggregator forwards the E2E Path across the region with the protocol number RSVP-E2E-IGNORE. When it reaches the deaggregator, that router should update the Path message's ADSPEC to reflect the effect of the region on achievable quality of service, using the ADSPEC of an aggregate Path. If no aggregate Path exists for the needed DSCP, the deaggregator sends an E2E PathErr with error code NEW-AGGREGATE-NEEDED and the DSCP in a DCLASS object. This is not a fatal error and removes no Path state. It asks the aggregator to start an aggregate Path.

When the E2E Resv arrives, the deaggregator makes the final choice of aggregate reservation, checks that enough bandwidth is reserved, and may first try to enlarge the aggregate. If it creates a new aggregate Resv, the message should be delivered reliably, using the mechanisms in RFC 2961 or the CONFIRM object. The deaggregator then forwards the E2E Resv to the aggregator with a DCLASS object naming the DSCP. The aggregator records the mapping, removes the DCLASS object and passes the Resv on.

On the data path, the aggregator marks packets of a mapped flow with the right DSCP. It also polices each E2E flow against its own token bucket. Out-of-profile packets must be dropped, reshaped or marked to a different DSCP. When E2E reservations go away, their FLOWSPEC and SENDER_TSPEC information is removed from the aggregate. If an aggregate reservation itself goes away, the E2E reservations it supports are no longer active.

The RFC also says the procedures can be used without any E2E RSVP at all, for example with a statically configured aggregate between two routers, or between two PSTN gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The exit router says, 'I need a group pass for this lane.' The entrance router books it. Once the pass exists, new kids just get added to it without bothering anyone in the middle.

sections.title: Protocol Elements
sections.content:
The RFC adds a handful of protocol elements: the IP protocol RSVP-E2E-IGNORE, the PathErr code NEW-AGGREGATE-NEEDED, and new object formats.

The SESSION object carries the aggregate session destination address and the DSCP. For unicast, the address is that of the deaggregating router. For multicast, it is the multicast address of the aggregated E2E session. When a session uses a pair of PHBs, such as AF11 and AF12, the DSCP of the numerically smallest one is used. IPv4 and IPv6 forms exist (C-Types RSVP-AGGREGATE-IP4 and RSVP-AGGREGATE-IP6). The SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC objects carry the aggregator's address.

The Router Alert option is also used for nested aggregation. E2E reservations are level 0, and a router that aggregates level n reservations into level n+1 writes n+1 in the 2-byte router alert field. A deaggregator only processes messages whose field carries the matching level.
sections.plainLanguage: These are new labels on the forms the routers pass around: one says 'ignore me until the exit', one says 'please start a group pass', and one names which router made the group pass.

sections.title: Sizing the Aggregate Reservation
sections.content:
A simple rule is that the aggregate must be at least the sum of the bandwidths of the E2E reservations, and its burst capacity at least the sum of theirs. But resizing on every change would throw away the main benefit, which is lower message processing in the region.

So the RFC assumes a policy, which it leaves to the operator, that keeps the aggregate stable. It suggests that the bandwidth needed is the larger of a requirement known in advance (such as a daily pattern) and the trend line over recent history, at 90 or 99% statistical confidence. Changes should be made no more often than every few minutes, ideally at granularities such as fifteen minutes or hourly. The aggregate would normally be an integer multiple of some block size, not exactly the sum. Some hysteresis is advised so the size does not oscillate.

The aggregator should include a SENDER_TSPEC in the aggregate Path that is at least as large as what the deaggregator may need, since a reservation cannot exceed the Path's SENDER_TSPEC. The deaggregator MAY grow or create aggregates ahead of demand.
sections.plainLanguage: When you book tables at a restaurant for a big group, you guess how many will show up and book a few extra. You do not call back every time one more person says yes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says losing an aggregate reservation to an attacker would make many calls run unreserved, and over-reserving bandwidth could cause denial of service, but these risks exist in RSVP itself. It also notes that the hop-by-hop INTEGRITY object of RSVP can be used. Because E2E messages skip the interior routers, the aggregator and deaggregator act as RSVP neighbors and must share a secret.

One risk is specific to aggregation. If the IP protocol number in a Path message were maliciously changed, later devices would ignore the message and reservations would fail. The value could even be corrected before it reached the receiver, hiding the attack. The RFC suggests an IPsec authentication header as a mitigation, at the cost of key management. It RECOMMENDS that implementations only change the protocol number for Path, PathTear and ResvConf, and that a general facility for this SHOULD NOT be offered.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy swaps the sticker on your ticket, the guards in the middle will ignore you. So routers should only be allowed to swap stickers on the three kinds of tickets that need it.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned IP protocol number 134 to RSVP-E2E-IGNORE and RSVP error code 26 to NEW-AGGREGATE-NEEDED. It assigned C-Type 9 to RSVP-AGGREGATE-IP4 and C-Type 10 to RSVP-AGGREGATE-IP6, with the same numbers in the Session, Filter Specification and Sender Template classes.

For IPv6, where the Router Alert value acts as an option sub-type, IANA assigned a block of 32 values (3-35, called Aggregated Reservation Nesting Level) that map to nesting depths 0 to 31.
sections.plainLanguage: The number registry gave each new label its own number, so every router reads them the same way.
